opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated questions in the field, partly because I'm a bit of an example of it myself. I didn't come up through the traditional PhD pipeline, and a lot of the people I most respect in ML didn't either.

The thing I look for most is evidence of agency and taste in what someone chose to work on when nobody told them to. If someone has gone off and reimplemented a paper from scratch, or found some weird bottleneck in a training run and chased it down, or built something end to end because they were curious, that tells you far more than a credential does. Formal ML training mostly gives you vocabulary and a set of priors, and you can pick those up pretty quickly if you're sharp and motivated. What's much harder to teach is the instinct to keep pulling on a thread until you actually understand what's going on.

The second thing is engineering ability, which I think people still undervalue. So much of frontier ML right now is really systems work: making things run fast, debugging distributed training, understanding why your loss curve did something strange at step forty thousand. Someone who's a genuinely excellent engineer, who is comfortable going down to the metal and reasoning about hardware and memory and communication, often ends up being more productive than someone with a beautiful theoretical background who can't ship.

Third, I look at how fast they learn. You can test this pretty directly. Give someone a problem slightly outside their comfort zone and watch how they approach it. Do they ask good questions? Do they build a mental model and then update it when it breaks? The slope matters more than the intercept.

And honestly, a lot of it is just that public work is a fantastic signal now. Blog posts, open-source contributions, a really thoughtful write-up of an experiment. If someone has done something publicly that impresses people who know the field, that's often the clearest possible demonstration, and it lets people without the traditional pedigree get noticed. I'd encourage anyone in that position to just go do the work in the open. The field is still young enough that a few months of serious, focused effort can get you to the frontier on some narrow problem, and people will notice.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, partly because I'm one of those people. I didn't come up through a PhD program, I came from a background that was pretty adjacent but not formally ML, and I think the thing that mattered was less what I knew at the time and more the slope I was on.

The way I'd frame it is that the field moves fast enough that the stock of knowledge someone has today depreciates really quickly. What doesn't depreciate is whether they can take a vague problem, decompose it, run experiments against it, and update honestly when the experiments tell them they were wrong. That loop, hypothesize, test, be surprised, revise, is basically the whole job. And you can see evidence of it in people who've never touched a transformer. Someone who spent two years obsessively optimizing a game engine, or a physics student who built their own simulation stack from scratch, or someone who got weirdly deep on a hobby project, those people have demonstrated that they'll run the loop without anyone telling them to.

So concretely, what I look for is a few things. One is just raw agency. Did this person go and do things nobody asked them to do? Did they hit a wall and route around it? That shows up in side projects, in weird open source contributions, in the fact that they taught themselves something hard because they wanted to, not for a credential. Two is technical depth in something, anything. It almost doesn't matter what. If someone has gone really deep on compilers or distributed systems or numerical methods, they've proven they can hold a complex system in their head, and ML is just another complex system. Honestly, the systems and infrastructure people are some of the most valuable hires right now, because so much of frontier research is really an engineering problem about making things run efficiently at scale. Three is intellectual honesty and taste. When you talk to them about a problem they worked on, do they know what they don't know? Do they volunteer the places where they got lucky or where their approach was hacky? That's a big signal, because a lot of research is about not fooling yourself.

The interview process I think works best is just giving people a real problem and watching them work on it, ideally over days rather than an hour on a whiteboard. Trial work, paid projects, something where you can see how they actually think when things don't go to plan. Credentials are a noisy proxy for all of this, and in a field where the frontier is like three years old, the proxy is especially noisy. The best people I've worked with have been remarkably uncorrelated with where they went to school or whether they did a PhD. What they share is that they're relentless and they're honest with themselves, and I'd take that over a stack of publications most days.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to distinguish between someone who hasn’t done machine learning and someone who can’t learn machine learning. Those are very different things. If somebody has become exceptionally good at another technical field, especially one where they’ve had to build things and get feedback from reality, that’s a strong signal.

Then I’d give them a concrete problem and work through it with them. Can they form a hypothesis, run an experiment, and figure out what the result actually tells them? When something doesn’t work, do they investigate it systematically? And if you give them a new piece of information, how quickly do they incorporate it?

You learn much more from that than from whether they know the names of the latest techniques. Someone with experience will obviously start ahead. But you’re hiring for what the person will contribute over the next few years, so their rate of learning matters enormously.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look for evidence that they can pick up something difficult and get unusually far with it. Have they built something impressive? Have they gone deep on a problem without somebody telling them what to do? A formal ML background is one way to demonstrate that, but it’s not the only way.

Then I’d work through a concrete problem with them. Give them enough context to get started and see how they reason: what questions they ask, how they test an idea, what they do when the result contradicts their intuition. You’re trying to distinguish someone who knows the vocabulary from someone who can actually figure things out.

For somebody coming from another field, the interesting thing is how quickly they close the gap. If you explain something and they immediately start drawing useful implications from it, that’s a much stronger signal than whether they’ve encountered that particular concept before.
